first.rationale: The two declining metrics are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), so the highest-leverage single slot is one that attacks the funnel directly rather than one that answers the competitor's price move. memory_73 is the explicit trap here: promotional pricing has real acquisition/revenue lift and would feel like the natural counter to aggressive entry pricing, but the same record says it materially reduced 30-day retention and warns against generalizing it. Under a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, that is a disqualifier, not a tradeoff to re-litigate. Referral incentives (memory_57) are clean but target established customers and do nothing for the two metrics that are actually degrading; enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) addresses a segment that is not the one under pressure. That leaves simplify_onboarding (memory_86) and activation_messaging (memory_91), which is exactly why I am spending both verification pulls on those two rather than on the pricing memory I have already decided not to act on. I want the original records because both are consolidated summaries whose effect sizes, populations, and durability windows are compressed away: memory_86 reports 'improved completion and time-to-value' across self-serve accounts, but I need to know whether the lift persisted past the first week and whether it was measured on the same SMB population now being poached. memory_91 is the newer memory (day 61) and closer to current conditions, so if its effect is larger or better-measured than memory_86's I will switch. I am also flagging a downstream value risk on the intended action: shortening onboarding can improve completion while stripping steps that qualify accounts or teach the product, converting a completion-rate win into lower-quality revenue — the same shape of failure as the pricing result. So the experiment must be instrumented on 30-day retention and qualified-revenue-per-account, not on completion rate alone, and I will treat a completion lift with flat or negative downstream quality as a failure. Standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout: the supporting evidence is direct but is 24 days old and predates the current competitive shift, and the declines may share an upstream cause that neither memory addresses.

final.rationale: Both verifications came back confirmed, and the specific downstream-quality risk I flagged before pulling the records was retired rather than confirmed: exp_86 shows shortened onboarding lifted completion +13% and cut time-to-value by 2.1 days while 30-day retention went UP 3%. That is the opposite of the promotional-pricing failure mode, where acquisition gains were paid for out of retention. So the worry that a completion-rate win would be bought by stripping qualifying or teaching steps is not supported by the source record, and I am lowering the flag rather than leaving it up as reflexive hedging. I am choosing simplify_onboarding over activation_messaging even though activation is the larger decline (-6%) and exp_91 posted an activation lift of exactly +6%. Three reasons. First, retention: exp_86 delivered +3% on 30-day retention versus +1% for exp_91, and under a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue the retention differential is the term that compounds. Second, ordering: onboarding completion sits upstream of activation, and both metrics are down together, which is consistent with the activation decline being partly a downstream shadow of the onboarding decline. Fixing the upstream constraint can recover both; messaging at the activation step treats the symptom and would be partly wasted if accounts are dropping before they reach it. Third, time-to-value: -2.1 days is the most direct defense available against a competitor's aggressive entry pricing, because it shortens the window in which a price-sensitive SMB account is still paying without having seen value. That is a durable answer to the competitive threat, whereas matching on price is the one move memory_73 explicitly warns against generalizing — its acquisition and revenue lift came with a material 30-day retention hit, and I am declining it despite it being the most direct-seeming counter to the competitor. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving: both source records are from days 52 and 61 and predate the current competitive shift, so the populations they measured were not being actively poached; the two declines may also share an upstream cause (traffic mix, a shipped regression) that neither memory speaks to and that this experiment would not diagnose. That is why I am running a standard experiment rather than a broad rollout. Instrumentation holds regardless of the lowered flag: I will read 30-day retention and qualified-revenue-per-account alongside completion, and treat a completion lift with flat or negative downstream quality as a failure, not a partial win. If the effect does not replicate against the current SMB mix, activation_messaging is the next slot, since exp_91 is confirmed, newer, and independently positive.
